name: Dusty purple tone
lede: Dusty purple tone is an English rendering of Futa'ai (二藍), a traditional Japanese name meaning "dark indigo", applied here to a greyed violet.

sections.title: A dark-indigo name for a greyed violet
sections.body:
Our color library lists this name as the English rendering of 二藍 (Futa'ai), "dark indigo", from the traditional colors of Japan [1]. The library gives the kanji and the meaning but no first-recorded date, so when the name entered use is undocumented here [1].

The hex itself (#614E6E) reads as a dusty, muted [[purple]] rather than the blue "indigo" the name points to [1]. That gap between a historical name and its modern screen swatch is common among the traditional names, which our library flags for checking against the dye rather than the pixel [1]. The nearest named color in our graph is [[madder-violet]], at a color distance (ΔE2000) of 2.6, almost the same shade; [[anthracene-violet]] sits 3.4 away and reads more vivid, and [[imperial-purple]] is 4.6 away, purpler and more vivid still [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this violet in only 22 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.1 percent, as photographed [3]. Its single biggest source is Impressionist and Post-Impressionist landscape painting from the 1890s, led by John Singer Sargent, whose canvases carry it at eleven times the archive's overall rate [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the count is a color match, not a pigment identification [3].

questions.q: What does the Japanese name behind Dusty purple tone, Futa'ai, literally mean?
True or false: the modern swatch for Dusty purple tone looks like the blue that its name describes.

openers: Dusty purple tone's name literally means "dark indigo", though the swatch reads as violet, not blue.

issues: No concordance hits; no first-recorded date available for the Japanese source name, left undocumented.
